summary:
Abuja Federal Capital Territory stands under Nigeria's national framework with no territorial carve-out. Nigeria criminalises same-sex conduct nationally under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA), and the law reaches far beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) documents that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Sexual orientation and gender identity carry criminal exposure at entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, while Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed: Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, and whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Abuja itself is the site of a documented trans-specific killing. On 8 August 2024 the beaten, bruised body of 33-year-old transgender TikToker "Abuja Area Mama" was found along the Katampe-Mabushi expressway in the Banex/Wuse II area, hours after she posted a final video, having previously expressed fear for her life. A police statement described the victim as "a man fully dressed in female clothing with no means of identification". Abuja police chief Benneth Igweh ordered a "thorough and discreet" investigation; The Dial (February 2025) records that six months later no suspects had been charged. A petition of nearly 6,000 signatures demands that her murder be investigated as a hate crime.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters (19 August 2026), warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states. The advisory extends the law to people who help arrange or conduct same-sex marriages and to activities involving gay groups and organisations, and warns that breaching curfews or movement restrictions could expose travellers to arrest and detention.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people. Although Nigerian laws guarantee freedom from discrimination, mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common, especially in northern states.
tangentialFactors:
Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case surfaced in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, which she served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Cross-dressing is banned under Sharia in the northern states and in the Nigerian military, and there is no legal route to change gender in Nigeria.
localsOnly:
Residents of the Federal Capital Territory live under the SSMPA's full penalty range, including 10 to 14 years for same-sex cohabitation, public display of a same-sex amorous relationship and running a gay organisation, alongside the colonial-era offence of "carnal knowledge against the order of nature" carrying up to 14 years.

Nigeria provides no legal route to change gender, so identity documents cannot be aligned with a trans person's lived gender; the police description of Abuja Area Mama as a man in female clothing indicates how authorities record gender in practice.

Mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common, particularly in the northern states, and the SSMPA has been used by police to justify torture and arbitrary arrest. Sharia-based cross-dressing bans apply in the twelve northern states and within the Nigerian military.

Placement of a trans detainee between male and female prison sections is left to official discretion; the October 2024 panel that reviewed the Bobrisky case found her maximum-security housing unlawful under the Nigerian Correctional Service Act but did not establish a general placement rule.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing reported by Reuters in September 2022 have been enacted is unresolved in the sources available here; the sources do not confirm any such statute in force in the Federal Capital Territory.

No Abuja-specific enforcement statistics, arrest figures or prosecution records for SSMPA offences are sourced; the Federal Capital Territory's own police practice is illustrated only by the Area Mama investigation and by national reporting on police extortion.

The outcome of the nearly 6,000-signature petition demanding that the Area Mama killing be investigated as a hate crime is not sourced, and no hate-crime charging provision applicable to her case is documented.

Whether the promised "thorough and discreet" investigation has produced any charge after the six-month point recorded in February 2025 is unresolved in these sources.

No source addresses which prison section a trans detainee would be held in within the Federal Capital Territory's facilities, or whether any policy exists there.
